title: Knowing when to move on: why Ryan Hoover left a good job at PlayHaven
summary: Ryan Hoover explains why he left a well-paid, growing startup role after nearly three years. His top priority is learning, and he'd lost passion for the market. He closes with three questions he uses to evaluate his next opportunity.

principles.text: Make learning your number one priority when deciding whether to stay or go.
principles.quote: my #1 priority is to learn. I’ve grown a _ton_ in the past three years, especially during times of [discomfort](http://ryanhoover.me/post/42414716750/fear-is-healthy) when I am challenged the most.

principles.text: If you don't look back at your past self with embarrassment, you've stopped growing.
principles.quote: When you look back at yourself six months from today and don’t feel embarrassed by your naiveté, there’s a problem. That means you’re not learning, growing.

principles.text: Lost passion for the market is a valid reason to leave, even when pay, growth and team are great.
principles.quote: But if I am to be honest with myself, I’ve lost passion for the market and industry we’re in.

principles.text: Builders who are their own user have an advantage: they understand the problem and persevere longer.
principles.quote: People that build products for themselves have a tremendous advantage because they _are_ their own user.

principles.text: A role narrowing from generalist to specialist can signal it's time to move on.
principles.quote: my role has become more specialized from my generalist roots.

principles.text: Evaluate opportunities with three questions: want, passion, and growth.
principles.quote: Is this really what I want to do? Am I (strongly) passionate about the product, market, and vision? Will I be challenged, learn, and grow to my full potential?
